t: Ieyasu fought on the plain against the advice of his own generals and of the Oda officers sent to help him, although Shingen had wished to avoid conflict and save his forces for Oda Nobunaga.

Tokugawa arquebusiers opened the battle, but Takeda cavalry rapidly overran Honda Tadakatsu's segment on the Tokugawa right, and a second cavalry charge followed by the Takeda main body drove the Tokugawa army into disorderly retreat.
Ieyasu returned to Hamamatsu with only five men and ordered the gates left open and braziers lit; the Takeda vanguard took this for a trap and camped for the night.
dyk: When Ieyasu reached Hamamatsu Castle, he is said to have ordered the gates left open and braziers lit, while Sakai Tadatsugu beat a large war drum. The Takeda vanguard took it for a trap and stopped to make camp.
ev: Aoyama Tadamon, a vassal of Ieyasu, resists the Takeda invasion of Mikawa and is later killed by a gunshot
Shingen leads 30,000 men south from Kōfu into Tōtōmi while Yamagata Masakage leads 5,000 into eastern Mikawa, and they take Yoshida Castle and Futamata Castle
The Tokugawa vanguard meets Yamagata Masakage and Baba Nobuharu at the Battle of Hitokotosaka
Ieyasu draws up his forces on the plain of Mikatagahara, and Takeda cavalry overrun the Tokugawa right and the Oda reinforcements
A second Takeda cavalry charge and the Takeda main body drive the Tokugawa army into retreat, and Ieyasu flees to Hamamatsu
That night about 100 Tokugawa foot soldiers and 16 matchlock gunners attack the Takeda camp and Shingen decides to withdraw
Shingen is fatally wounded at the Siege of Noda Castle

f.date: 25 January 1573; in the Japanese calendar the 22nd day of the 12th month of the 3rd year of Genki
f.place: The plain of Mikatagahara, north of Hamamatsu, in Tōtōmi Province, in present-day Shizuoka Prefecture, Japan
f.sides: The Takeda under Takeda Shingen, who led 30,000 men south in October 1572 while Yamagata Masakage led a second force of 5,000 into eastern Mikawa; the Tokugawa under Tokugawa Ieyasu, with 8,000 men at Hamamatsu Castle plus 3,000 reinforcements from Oda Nobunaga. The Kōyō Gunkan says Shingen outnumbered Ieyasu three to one.
f.outcome: The Tokugawa and Oda force was almost totally destroyed and many of Ieyasu's retainers were killed. Ieyasu escaped to Hamamatsu Castle with five men, and a night attack by his remaining men helped persuade Shingen to withdraw.
